column1: TCS SSS - Assess Proper Document Location for Calculations used by the TCS
column37:
During Peer Review of RCR-4477, J. Sevigny pointed out that the TCS SSS was missing a requirement to use seawater density recevied from SCS in the liquid level calculation specifically during ATN CONOPs when the bottom hatch is opening and perforimg Water Level Control.

 

The resolution to this comment was deferred as D. LaMotte disagreed over the simple addition of a requirement and would require further context to be added such as the following equation is used to caclulate T9 LL...

The TCS shall use desnity of sea water for liquid level calculations when the T9 BH is open. NOTE: The TCS uses density of sea water when the hatch is open since the seawater will be mixing with the water used to initally fill the tube.

 

Resolution to the comnment was deferred and the level of information pointed out above should be added to a lower level document (TCAP SRS). All the SSS needs to convey is that the seawater desnity is received and drive the capturing of when it is used in the liquid level calcualtion in a lower level document.

NOTE: Sea water density values should be from the SC sensors used in the Sail. There is an issue of values being stale due to the way they register changes in the ship's movement from those located in the keel and has been corrected for those in the Sail

column1: TCS SSS - (PTR needs to be made) Document Needs to Address Sensor Mark Down Requirements and Incorporate Into the Document
column37:
During review of RCR-4139, J. Sevigny commented that the TCS SSS is lacks in it's ability to convey what sensors are marked down and which are not via requirements. For example. if a sensor is marked down its not being used as part of the BH state, the sensor should then be displayed as faulted.

 

This was deferred and to be made into a PTR specific to sensor selection. This needs to encompass the problem of needing to mark down as sensor from interlock logic and operation should it be deemed to have failed/is faulted. The problem also extend to the implemenation of a bypass feature as it relates to indications/states dependent upon a single sensor/signal like the Tube 10 bottom hatch locking ring.

This should be addressed holistically and then broken down into pieces if needed

column1: RCR 4137 - Tube 9-to-sea DP Over Pressurization Caution
column37: The TCS will need a caution to generate when internal Tube 9 pressure at the location of the lower SAPTs is greater than or equal to (TBD) psi of calculated sea pressure external to Tube 9 at the same location as the lower SAPTs. It is needed to notify an operator that Tube 9 internal pressure exceeds the intended pressure due to malfunction of the TCS, the external hydraulic system, or the ATN system. This could lead to  possible hatch assembly damage, air potentially escaping from Tube 9, damage to pressure-compensated components within Tube 9 (either shipboard components or components that are part of a Tube 9 GFE), and unintentional flooding of Tube 9. The internal Tube 9-to-sea DP at which an alarm is generated to indicate that Tube 9 internal pressure exceeds the designed pressure has not been determined.

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260610-03: Addition of Requirement to Track LPT Calibration
column37: A comment during the PI17 review stated that it may be beneficial to track the total amount of calibration performed on an LPT to help inform rope stretch. Essentially, each time an LPT is calibrated, the baseline is set to what the LPT is currently reading. By tracking the total amount of inches the LPT reading has shifted from the nominal baseline for the zero position, the total amount of rope stretch can be calculated.

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-250716-01: Component Actuation Times
column37:
During TCS SSS CDR Project Leads Review, a comment pointed out that TCS products are missing a central location for gaining agreement on component actuation times with all relevant external stakeholders such as hydraulics, mechanical, etc.

Due to the TCS CONOPs being the document intended to establish stakeholders agreement of operations in support of TCS requirements development and that the document is reviewed by all relevant external stakeholders, the TCS COD needs to be updated to include component actuation times

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-250626-01: Tube Equalization to Sea
column37: The current tube equalization to sea description states that the equalization to sea indication and calculation is based solely on the upper or lower SAPT no.1 (dependent upon the hatch that is going to be opened)in the respective tube. This would cause the TCS to be unable to determine equalization to sea if the upper or lower SAPT no.1 in the respective tube were to fail. The TCS COD needs to be updated to resolve this issue and ensure tube equalization is updated to the latest system design

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-250617-01: Updating FD CONOPs
column37: The current FD CONOPs conflicts with the gravity fill permissive logic for Tube 10. TD-814 is required to be in the DRAIN position prior to opening TD-801-(10) and TD-802-(10) and in order to send the permissive both of these valves need to be open. The current FD CONOPs in the TCS COD does not change TD-814 to the DRAIN position until after TD-801-(10) and TD-802-(10) are opened and the permissive is sent. The TCS COD needs to be updated to ensure TD-814 is aligned to correct position prior to opening TD-801-(10) and TD-802-(10) as well as ensure the rest of the FD CONOPs is updated to reflect the most up to date system design

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-250523-02: VST Access Hatch Updates
column37: The TCS CONOPs document incorrectly states the VST access hatches hold-open pins automatically engage and is missing that the VST upper hatch padlock also has a stowage location near the hold-open levers on the IBT wall once the lock is removed from the hatch itself during opening. The descriptions and procedures relating to the VST Access Hatches need to be updated to reflect the most up to date system design

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260707-01: Updates to requirements for stopping hatch movement
column37:
The current wording in TCS_3525 needs to be updated to clearly identify what is required to stop a hatch mid sequence. Currently the requirement states: "The TCS shall remove any active command to a hatch when the associated interlock logic is violated."
However, the "interlock logic" this is referring to is enable logic which should be different from stopping hatch movement. This requirement would result in unintended behavior such as stopping the tube 9 bottom hatch that is in transition (already opened) when the aligned to sea state was lost, even though that condition is only needed to initiate the open sequence. Once the hatch is opened the loss of the aligned to sea state does not create a safety mishap.

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260428-34: Confirm the duration over which the TCS will average the calculated instantaneous liquid level to enable the TCS to add or remove air from Tube 9 in response to changes in average liquid level but not in response to oscillations i...
column37:
The objective of the ATN sub-mode WLC functionality is to actively maintain the air bubble in Tube 9 such that the average liquid level at the gas-liquid interface always remains within a designated safe band when the bottom hatch is not shut. While Tube 9 is pressurized and the bottom hatch is open, it is expected that changes to the conditions in Tube 9 could cause the time averaged liquid level in the tube to rise or fall (e.g., a GFE system installed in Tube 9 could generate enough heat to raise the nominal air temperature in the tube, thereby increasing pressure of the air, pushing the average liquid level lower). The instantaneous liquid level heights caused by slight changes in trim and list and SHS depth error are filtered out by the time average calculation to avoid cycling between pressurizing and venting; avoiding cycling minimizes air usage. The duration over which the TCS will average the calculated instantaneous liquid level (to avoid reacting to a single liquid level outside of the band and account for hovering and oscillations that may drive liquid level back into the band without needing to add or remove air from Tube 9) needs to be confirmed.

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260428-30: Confirm the Tube 9 equalization backup time delay for Tube 9 full flood CONOPs
column37:
Currently, the TCS includes a backup equalization method that uses a time delay to determine equalization of Tube 9 pressure and external sea pressure during full flood operations. In the event of multiple SAPT failure in Tube 9, the TCS cannot sense pressure inside the tube to compare with the calculated Tube 9 sea pressure to determine tube equalization. As a back-up operation, the TCS determines equalization through a timing method. This is done through a fixed time delay that ensures tube equalization has occurred and is based on the worst-case scenario equalization time across all operating depths for Tube 9 hatch-operating missions. Additionally, an indication is provided to operators when the timing method was used instead of the normal comparative method. The backup time delay is pending finalization of Tube 9 full flood CONOPs.

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260428-35
column37: |VA-SSW-PHC-260428-35|4|200(A)| |Bottom hatch status/state logic updates|Currently, a faulted SELS or LPT would stop the bottom hatch mid sequence. If this occurs during ATN CONOPs there is a possibility of not triggering WLC when opening the bottom hatch or PC intermediate when shutting the bottom hatch, due to an falsely identified unknown hatch state. Since these functions are triggered by the bottom hatch status during open and shut sequences the bottom hatch status logic needs to be updated to allow continued operations in the event of sensor failure. While the issue was discovered for Tube 9 ATN CONOPs the same logic can be applied to Tube 10 bottom hatch. A failed SELS or LPT should not immediately stop the hatch sequence or cause the state to be unknown if the TCS can determine the state. This logic also applies to the locking ring status/state.|

column37: |VA-SSW-PHC-260508-01|4|200(A)| |Specify the difference between a non-critical and critical fault for ATN faults|During TCS SSS alignment to the TCS SIS, Test commented that an alarm and caution is not explicitly stated for PM/FL requirements in the TCS SSS. column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260707-01
column37:
|VA-SSW-PHC-260707-01|4|100(P)| |Updates to requirements for stopping hatch movement|The current wording in TCS_3525 needs to be updated to clearly identify what is required to stop a hatch mid sequence. Currently the requirement states: "The TCS shall remove any active command to a hatch when the associated interlock logic is violated."
However, the "interlock logic" this is referring to is enable logic which should be different from stopping hatch movement. This requirement would result in unintended behavior such as stopping the tube 9 bottom hatch that is in transition (already opened) when the aligned to sea state was lost, even though that condition is only needed to initiate the open sequence. Once the hatch is opened the loss of the aligned to sea state does not create a safety mishap.|

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260714-01
column37: |VA-SSW-PHC-260714-01|4|100(P)| |Update TCS_2151 with surge findings|During our bottom hatch state logic surge meetings we determined that TCS_2151 (When no commands are active, the TCS shall have a control to energize all normally energized hydraulic control valve solenoids) this could cause unintended hatch movement. If the hatch was open or in transition and the TCS lost connection to the NIOU, after connection is reestablished, this control would be available. The normally energized solenoids are shut and locked when the hatch is open these solenoids should be deenergized. Update the requirement so it doesn't cause unintended movement.|

Supporting requirements like display requirements should also be added where applicable.|

column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260610-03 - Add Requirement to Track LPT Calibration
column37: |VA-SSW-PHC-260610-03|4|200(A)| |A comment during the PI 17 review stated that it may be beneficial to track the total amount of calibration performed on an LPT to help inform rope stretch. column1: VA-SSW-PHC-260428-34

|VA-SSW-PHC-260428-34|4|200(A)| |Confirm the duration over which the TCS will average the calculated instantaneous liquid level to enable the TCS to add or remove air from Tube 9 in response to changes in average liquid level but not in response to oscillations in instantaneous liquid level.|The objective of the ATN sub-mode WLC functionality is to actively maintain the air bubble in Tube 9 such that the average liquid level at the gas-liquid interface always remains within a designated safe band when the bottom hatch is not shut. While Tube 9 is pressurized and the bottom hatch is open, it is expected that changes to the conditions in Tube 9 could cause the time averaged liquid level in the tube to rise or fall (e.g. GFE system installed in Tube 9 could generate enough heat to raise the normal air temperature in the tube, thereby increasing pressure of the air, pushing the average liquid level lower). The instantaneous liquid level heights caused by slight changes in trim and list and SHS depth error are filtered out by the time average calculation to avoid cycling between pressurizing and venting; avoiding cycling minimizes air usage. The duration over which the TCS will average the calculated instantaneous liquid level (to avoid reacting to a single liquid level outside of the band and account for hovering and oscillations that may drive liquid level back into the band without needing to add or remove air from Tube 9) needs to be confirmed.

column1: TCS CAD - Discuss w/ D456 Electrical Cableways & D465 EHPs on Tube 9/10 Cabling Issue and Potential for a Side Study
column37:
On June 12th, D440 reached out to D456 Outboard Electrical Cableways on the feasibility on changing cable types in Tube 9 and Tube 10 to the alternate cables suitable for a high-pressure air environment. 

Upon initial looks D456 stated that
 * the two lower electrodes would be the most difficult to  accommodate with the bend radius growing four inches, the inline connectors would have to be moved further away and there is a nearby camera foundation limiting that. Might require some adjustment of the sensor location or foundation.
 * It would require re-design of several cableways to accommodate the increase in OD and bend radius throughout the arrangment
 * We would need to check in w/ D465 EHPs if the cable change affect the EHPs or EHP connectors
 * Other than that saw no showstoppers

D440 requested additional clarification from D456 if modifying the cable type in Tube 10 as well was checked and if changing to a 1SPR-16 improve the potential issues and the cost and time needed to redesign cableways.

Additionally, requested input from D465 on affects to the EHPs and EHP connector and if using 90 or 45 degree connectors prevent issues.

 

D465 stated for T9 changes that there would be no impacts to EHPs and some plugs could be updated but is pretty simple. Using the 1PSR-16 cable would be preferrable for the electrode cable due to the smaller diameter and bend radius than the 2SPR-16 cable

For Tube 9 lower electrodes use of a 90 degree connector per M24231/2 could alleviate bend radius concern.

 

Other cables in T9 would need to be assessed as well as Tube 10 like the L&R cabling

column1: RCR-4145 - Review Cycle
column37:
I spoke with Alex Padgett offline, and the conclusion was that it seems we’re missing requirements to point to for qualifying our sensors (sensors that fall under Systems ownership). This seems to align with the TCP SSS.

 

Regarding qualification requirements, Alex mentioned two ways we can cover this, both of which are done in the TCP SSS. One way is to have the requirement itself embedded within the TCP SSS, so that way the TCP SSS has the requirements components must meet to be considered “qualified”, you can see this in the EMC qual. section of the TCP SSS, where the requirements explicitly state what tests the sensor needs to pass, and what requirements they must conform with.

 

The other way to tackle this is to have a procurement spec, which the SSS can point to for qualification. Typically, when these sensors are bought, they come with OQE that give the test methods and results that prove the component is conforming to the qualification requirements in the procurement spec. Otherwise, if the vendor cannot provide this (due to not having the appropriate facilities), EB would need to go perform the applicable tests to see if the sensor meets the qualification requirements. Alex mentioned that this would more than likely be a joint effort between D440 Systems, and D440 Test to at least identify the appropriate groups we need to contact in order to conduct these tests (for example, we work with D477 for EMC related requirements, like we just did for the EST LPTs).

 

In both of these cases, the requirements are pretty much derived from the Ship Spec level, and it sounded like it’s on D440 Systems to go figure out what requirements we need to have for our sensors, and potentially which test methods to invoke. One other thing Alex had mentioned is that this information would more than likely live in our SSS in some way because these are components we own to inform the operation of the system (and we also happen to own them on our CAD as well).

 

Alex also showed me a couple of flowcharts for one of the systems he’s previously worked. Essentially, those had the logic flowcharts of the requirements. He was mentioning that the logic of the system itself is tested at FQT and SQT, so this would really just be our system level requirements (shall do X, Y, Z). I bring this up because this sounds like the equipment that we own would need to be qualified before FQT and SQT, because I’d assume we want to test our system level requirements with hardware that has been qualified, which we can only do if we qualify our system components before then (FQT and SQT) – I could be wrong here so this may be worth double checking, especially since FQT is very close, and we’d have to do quite a bit to get these requirements into our document somehow.

 

Alex, thank you again for sitting down and walking me through this – please feel free to correct anything I’ve written here, or add anything else.

 

Dylan, let me know your thoughts, but I think we should probably relay this to Adam in some form. I’ve spoke with Zack about most of this information earlier, so he’s pretty up to speed and I think he agrees that this is something we should be speaking to Adam about.

column1: Re-evaluate Interlocks Involving Pressure Transducers
column37: Currently, there are some interlocks that involve pressure transducer readings at a certain value before continuing on with operation. We want to look at if it is worth removing the pressure readings from the interlock, or restricting the combination of sensor indications to a single mode of operation (restricting it to only automatic mode, and have a separate interlock for the manual mode).

column1: Speak with J. Krause About Stalling Motors and Holding Tray Under Tension
column37: We want to discuss w/ J. Krause to go through some failure scenarios involving reeling into reduced stall. We want to know how long it takes for the reduced stall pressure to be achieved when the SELS are indicated as housed. This is in the even where the PX indication is lost. We also want to talk about holding the tray under tension within the bottom side fairing, just in case there is truly risk of hitting full stall of the motors.

column1: Reach Out to Vendor for LPT Calibration Periodicity
column37: We want to see how likely the LPTs are to drift from their original readings during their operational lifetime. This will be used to help inform some of the tolerance work we are looking into, and to determine how often the LPTs need to be replaced.

column1: Investigate the Failure Scenario of a SELS
column37: This task is to look at a failure scenario of the SELS during a CONOPs walkthrough. This could be during the Stow or Deploy sequences.

column1: Update Definition of Stowed
column37: The EST SSS currently establishes the Stowed position as a combination of coordinates, and the SELS housed indication. The Stowed position should only be a set of coordinates. While the SELS may be useful in the Stow operations of the tray, they are not a necessity for determining if the tray is at the Stowed position.

column1: Investigate Pressure Transducer Failure
column37: This task is for investigating a pressure transducer failure. Currently, it is unknown how a pressure transducer can fail. The current understanding is that if the pressure transducer fails, they will read "zero PSID", but this still falls within the allowable range. A fault will not get triggered and it is possible for the motors to indefinitely reel in without ever reaching the appropriate thresholds. We need to look into how the pressure transducers can fail, and how that would be identified.

column1: Investigate SELS Failure
column37: This task is for investigating a total failure of the SELS. Currently, the EST SSS examines the channel A and channel B on the same SELS. However, there is no way to assess if both channels of the SELS fail to the same position. We need to look into if this is possible to identify.

column1: Re-evaluate the Positional Tolerance of the LPTs
column37: EST SSS uses 1.0 inch universally for positional tolerance and synchronization tolerance (between drives, and between redundant sensors on the same drive. An inch provides very little room for pitch, may cause nuisance alarms/faults, so we want to verify if an inch is the correct value to establish as the tolerance.

column1: Reassess Fault Criticality of EST Faults
column37: Currently, nearly all faults in the EST SSS are marked as critical, which will prohibit movement when they are triggered. This leads to some non-catastrophic failure that cannot be resolved due to the restrictions of a critical fault.

column1: MIL-STD-1686 Applicability for TCS SAPTs
column37: A vendor has responded (Paroscientific) that they adhere to MIL-STD-1686C. This is not authorized for use by EB.
column43:
There are a couple points to this task.

 

In the end, it does not matter what the vendor has their components built to, at least not for 1686, because EB is not invoking any requirements on the vendor through something such as an EB spec. This request for modification would be done via a statement of work, at which point EB will perform the qualification testing.

Regarding 1686, it is true that EB only allows 1686B for use, per the VA MIRD and SEI, which the EMC group concurs with - they were the ones to provide that guidance.

The C15 form filled out by Paroscientific was provided accidentally by someone in 323, so that will have to be resolved on their end. The vendor should have never received this form because it is for internal auditing, so the fact that the vendor claims to have filled out this form is strange.

The existing EB specification that was used as a reference will need to be update, since the wrong standard is referenced for 1686, and also for MIL-STD-461.;19/May/26 5:39 PM;aly;12960

column1: SELS Investigation for FST
column37: This task is for looking into the SELS procurement for the FST. There is no current buyer assigned to the PO we submitted back in March.
column43:
There has been a lot of discussions and investigations regarding this topic.

 

We needed to contact TE, the EB buyers (Janee + Justin Z), the GDIT buyer (James) and Mike Baycura.

 

We needed to confirm that TE still makes the component, and is able to support production despite the chip being obsolete (to create the internal board of the SELS).

 

Then we needed to confirm that GDIT can make the SELS, they can, however they source their chips through the Navy. According to Baycura, these chips are only allowed for tactical use. With our PO being tied to a test event, GDIT will more than likely come back with a no bid because the SELS will be used as test assets - this no bid offer would likely come much further down the road, past the point where we needed to have purchased the component by.

 

Janee submitted the PO to GDIT and now needs to rescind the PO. Justin needs to take over the PO because he is the buyer for TE.;19/May/26 4:33 PM;aly;16920

column1: Investigation of MS3137 Connector
column37:
This affects the Tactical CAD and the FST, but the issue originates from FST.

 

We submitted a RFQ to Heilind ICC for an ms3137 connector, which was made by TE. TE states that the part is active, which is done on their site and via a phone call, so we were under the impression that they are still making the component. However, the RFQ came back as a no bid, because internally the component is actually marked as stop shipment (and therefore not in production) due to ongoing re-qual for the connector that they are not cognizant of.

 

We need to find an alternative vendor to see if this connector can be bought
column43:
After speaking w/ TE and some other vendors / distributors, we were able to find a company that manufactures the component, Robert Technologies Inc.

 

TE truly does not make this component anymore, and has not made the component in at least 5 years (unsure if this history goes farther). This now has email OQE stating that this component cannot be bought. Robert Technologies still makes the component, but we will need to look into this further to see if we should be proceeding forward with this solution, or make a larger push to change out the receptacle so that we can use a more standardized connector series that is not obsolete.;19/May/26 12:05 PM;aly;15120

column1: TD - IBTAB No. 7 Low Pressure Meeting 2
column37:
This is a 2nd follow on meeting with SC on the feasibility of adding an additional pressure transducer to their system. Additional items to be discussed is adding a manual gage to the ATN system should a 5 min valve line-up be insufficient and push back on taking a casualty line-up offline for a portion of time, and how this new information would be provided to TCS

 

Mike/Miles/Austin,

 

We discussed at the SCS FHA WG there is a new safety critical SCS hazard resulting from a fails to operate or degraded function malfunction failure mode of the IBTAB No. 7 pressure indication.
 * Currently there is no local indication or redundant sensor for the IBTAB No.7 however Miles did discuss there is some sort of lineup we can do to check the pressure.

 

For TCS the worst-case situation I want to investigate is that Water-level Control (WLC) is active AND the T9 High-level electrodes are WETTED.
 * The IBTAB No.7 low pressure is actually low or is incorrectly indicated.

 

What do we do at TCS at this point? Our only response currently is shut TD-803-(9) which doesn’t help our waterline, at this point we risk damaging the GFE system so realistically we shut the hatch.

 

The real question is how can we verify the IBTAB No. 7 pressure (valve lineup which utilizes manual valves and manual guage which could take say around 5 min)? Do we NEED another sensor or manual gauge at the IBTAB No. 7?

 

TCS SIS has a TBD in the TCS SIS to track this (any additional alerts/interlocks can be discussed at a later date), this is to determine if we need to add sensors to the IBTAB which would affect SCS. Or if we just make a new CONOPS step to verify the IBTAB No.7 before opening the hatch.

column1: RCR-4145 - TCS SSS  - Environmental Requirements Missing in TCS SSS
column37:
I spoke with Alex Padgett offline, and the conclusion was that it seems we’re missing requirements to point to for qualifying our sensors (sensors that fall under Systems ownership). This seems to align with the TCP SSS.

 

Regarding qualification requirements, Alex mentioned two ways we can cover this, both of which are done in the TCP SSS. One way is to have the requirement itself embedded within the TCP SSS, so that way the TCP SSS has the requirements components must meet to be considered “qualified”, you can see this in the EMC qual. section of the TCP SSS, where the requirements explicitly state what tests the sensor needs to pass, and what requirements they must conform with.

 

The other way to tackle this is to have a procurement spec, which the SSS can point to for qualification. Typically, when these sensors are bought, they come with OQE that give the test methods and results that prove the component is conforming to the qualification requirements in the procurement spec. Otherwise, if the vendor cannot provide this (due to not having the appropriate facilities), EB would need to go perform the applicable tests to see if the sensor meets the qualification requirements. Alex mentioned that this would more than likely be a joint effort between D440 Systems, and D440 Test to at least identify the appropriate groups we need to contact in order to conduct these tests (for example, we work with D477 for EMC related requirements, like we just did for the EST LPTs).

 

In both of these cases, the requirements are pretty much derived from the Ship Spec level, and it sounded like it’s on D440 Systems to go figure out what requirements we need to have for our sensors, and potentially which test methods to invoke. One other thing Alex had mentioned is that this information would more than likely live in our SSS in some way because these are components we own to inform the operation of the system (and we also happen to own them on our CAD as well).

 

Alex also showed me a couple of flowcharts for one of the systems he’s previously worked. Essentially, those had the logic flowcharts of the requirements. He was mentioning that the logic of the system itself is tested at FQT and SQT, so this would really just be our system level requirements (shall do X, Y, Z). I bring this up because this sounds like the equipment that we own would need to be qualified before FQT and SQT, because I’d assume we want to test our system level requirements with hardware that has been qualified, which we can only do if we qualify our system components before then (FQT and SQT) – I could be wrong here so this may be worth double checking, especially since FQT is very close, and we’d have to do quite a bit to get these requirements into our document somehow.

 

Alex, thank you again for sitting down and walking me through this – please feel free to correct anything I’ve written here, or add anything else.

 

Dylan, let me know your thoughts, but I think we should probably relay this to Adam in some form. I’ve spoke with Zack about most of this information earlier, so he’s pretty up to speed and I think he agrees that this is something we should be speaking to Adam about.

column1: TCS SSS/COD - Gravity Fill Permissive or Sequencing Update
column37:
*Requires some conversation with FD and then Incorporation into the document*

 

*Tube 10 Gravity Filling CONOPs Logic Issues*
 # Per current valve interlock logic and GRAVITY FILL READY permissive logic in the TCS SSS and TCS SIS documents, TD-801/802-(10) are unable to be/remain open unless TD-814 (SC operated valve) was aligned to the DRAIN position. The GRAVITY FILL READY permissive is unavailable to select unless TD-801/802-(10) are OPEN. 
 # Currently initial conditions require TD-803/804-(10) and TD-815 to be OPEN prior to an operator entering the VST and an operator being stationed in the VST is required for Gravity Filling, however, the Gravity Fill permissive logic requires these valves to be SHUT 
 # Per current valve interlock logic, step 16 of GRAVITY FILLING would cause TD-801/802-(10) to auto shut and results in auto removal of Gravity Fill Ready permissive

*Options to Resolve Issue 1: (Requires confirming this route w/ D413 FD team and adjusting the TCS COD to deconflict with the specification requirements)*
 # Move Step 9 of SC aligning TD-814 to the DRAIN position to step 7 prior to opening TD-801/802-(10)
 # Remove the TD-814 is aligned to DRAIN position (NOT DESIREABLE), lose dual isolation if this route is chosen

*Options to Resolve Issue 2: (Requires confirming this route w/ D413 FD team and adjusting the TCS COD to deconflict with the specification requirements)*
 # Add steps at the beginning of Gravity Filling to shut these valves to satisfy the permissive logic
 # Remove the vent valves being required shut to send the Gravity Fill Ready permissive. Due to the amount of liquid being used to fill the valve, these is not a clear reason that they need to be SHUT.
 ## Personnel are technically inside of the VST during GRAVITY Filling, so if T9 was pressurized i.e. ATN ops and TD-853 failed open and those valves were left open then you could pressurize into T10 with personnel inside? However, you may just be directly pressurizing into the ship since the hatch would be open?
 ## Casualty Scenario of: T9 was prepped and opened first, then ship goes shallow causing water to enter tube vent piping and TD-853 was open (failed) causing flooding into T10/VST with personnel inside and an open access to ship? Probably miniscule chance of happening and relies on multiple failures needing to occur

*Options to Resolve Issue 3: (Requires confirming this route w/ D413 FD team and adjusting the TCS COD to deconflict with the specification requirements)*
 # Leave as-is and update CONOPs to reflect this design choice
 # Remove the TD-814 is aligned to DRAIN position (NOT DESIREABLE), lose dual isolation if this route is chosen

TD/TCS CAD - Fill out CWS SSW Risk Reporting Form for Tube 9 Bottom Hatch EMA Development and Provide to D440 Lead/D440 hardware
column37:
Background:

NIOU TUBES 9 & 10 has an interface with the Tube 9 EMA controller. In the wire table provided to GDIT, this has a single full-duplex RS-485 comms path and a 28VDC power supply and return pair. During Leads review of VA-SSW-SC-ICD-001 CP-0036 (3/19/26), Zach Pryor identified that there should be additional requirements for the Power On/Power Off discrete commands to the EMA. This prompted a discussion, where we noticed the discrepancy between the wire table and the intended pinout. Upon reviewing the procurement spec for the EMA controller, I identified some discrepancies between that document and the pinouts from Systems, i.e. that the EB-Spec had 2 RS-485 paths and no discrete commands compared to the 1 RS-485 and discrete on/off commands in the pinouts.

 

Problem:

D465 is still going through the vendor downselect process for the EMA controller, so while Zach has a draft pinout for the NIOU interface, we have not been able to confirm with the three vendors that they can all meet this interface. The most recent status I have (4/9/26) is that D440 will be able to review the updates to EB-6668 when it goes into review next, but we have not received an ECD from D465 on that review. This review is also not positive confirmation that the eventually chosen vendor will be able to use the NIOU interface Zach has drafted.

 

GDIT is currently wiring NIOU TUBES 9 & 10 with the initial wire table EB provided. Every day that we do not send the updated wire table with the final pinouts increases the risk of GDIT needing to perform rework to correct this interface. Once Zach gets confirmation from D465 on the pinouts, I will have to work with the HW team to get the NIOU wire table updated, at which point we can send that to GDIT and then review their electrical schematic, so there will still probably be a week delay after we confirm what the interface will be.

 

Highly recommend opening a risk (not a watch item) and tracking the mitigation steps and the impacts.

Very Respectfully,

Adam J. White

column1: (RES Deferred) TCS SSS - Update Move Timeout, Command Timeout, and Excessive Command Without Movement Timeouts to Include RES Sensor Info
column37:
Due to a change in methodology for TCS COD command timeout faults, this leads to the need for move timeout faults for all actuated components done by the TCS. This is to better differentiate/locate the fault and whether the component has failed to move vs, took too long to achieve the command position. Currently, the TCS SSS only has this for the bottom hatches that include LPTs and the RES sensors. This would need to be based off how long should it take to lose the current state after being commanded to a different state and not the full component actuation time.

 

In addition to updating move timeout faults, D413 suggested adding excessive command without movement faults like the EST SSS has to indicate earlier if the bottom hatches have stopped moving when it hasn't reached the commanded state. Including these faults would better differentiate and locate the fault that it stopped moving than if it reached the state too slowly. This would apply to any sensor that provides position versus just the end states:



"LPTs measure the position of the Tube 9 and Tube 10 bottom hatches and two EMAs measure the position of the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring. The LPTs and EMAs may identify a potential problem earlier than the command timeout faults should the sensors indicate motion has ceased before the Tube 9 and Tube 10 hatches or Tube 9 locking ring have reached the commanded state. The TCS detects an excessive command without movement fault when this occurs. This method is independent of system variables that affect actuation time, improving the connection between fault detection and the applicable failure. Further details on PM/FL and excessive command without movement faults are documented in the SSS for the TCS, reference 2.2 (d)."

column1: TCS COD (Possible Task?) - Update Component Actuation Times to Include TCS Processing Time in Groom Time
column37:
TCS COD Component Actuation Times Tables currently states:

"The purpose of a command timeout fault is to notify operators of a potential problem with actuation of components and therefore is based off the maximum groom time. The command timeout value includes the durations of all processes by which the component was groomed and excludes all processes that weren’t involved in grooming. For example, the command timeout value includes TCS processing time if actuation during grooming was accomplished via the TCS. TCS processing time is excluded if the component was groomed by manually operating the control valve. In general, the command timeout fault timer starts when the component is no longer in the initial state as indicated by its sensors.     Start and stop triggers for the command timeout fault and grooming procedures are identical or to the greatest extent possible. The table below does not include TCS processing times and further details on PM/FL and command timeout faults are documented in the SSS for the TCS, reference 2.2 (d)."

Depending on testing/grooming of the valves, if the TCS is used to groom and determine actuation times, then these times will need to be updated to include that extra time if any is needed

h2. *Hatch Sequencing/Interlocks:*

According to Appendix K of EB-4295 REV E, the TD-813 interlock includes a condition:

TD-805 is aligned to TUBE 9 and Tube 9 pressure is <1.5 psid from sea pressure and TD-803-(9) is SHUT and TD-801-(9) is OPEN

Rationale: Allows for a path to sea via the SSW ingestion CORD to support Tube 9 top/bottom hatch closure. 

There is a matching Tube 10 condition. This is not a problem for normal operations, but is an issue for ATN operations that require TD-803-(9) is OPEN

aligned to the SSW CORD position unless one of the

permissive (see Appendix N) is in place

pressure is <1.5 psid from sea pressure and
TD-803-(10) is SHUT or *TD-804-(10) is SHUT* (should make this suggestion for EB-6295) and TD-801-(10) is
OPEN

pressure is <1.5 psid from sea pressure and
TD-803-(9) is SHUT and TD-801-(9) is OPEN

column1: TD - Update Pinouts Per Discussion w/ D492 and Review of Updated datasheets for RES Sensors
column37:
Jamieson,

 

The sensor table for ICD 5710000 currently states that 2 of the contacts for the LVDTs are a 4-20mA supply and return which is consistent with the provided data sheet and what we currently are tracking. However, the data sheet also lists a Case Ground and 6 total possible contacts compared to the current 4 contacts listed. Additionally, the input voltage on the data sheet is listed as 12-28 VDC while the supply voltage listed in the sensor table is 28 +/- 2 VDC. I am not sure if there is some rationale for why they differ that Dylan and I are not aware of currently.

 

Acquiring a data sheet for the 301 model would be beneficial as we have the signals as Power (Supply) , Sensed (Normally Open), and Not sensed (Normally Closed) like the magnetic switches and that does not seem to match the sensor table which lists the signals as Signal (Active High) (Normally Open/Sensed), Supply (Power), and Return (Common) (Power Return, not Normally Closed/Not Sensed). It appears on the data sheet the model number may slightly change the signals whether the connection is 3 wire or 4 pin and the output on pin 2 and pin 4 and whether it is Normally open or Normally close. column37:
Dylan, Zach,

 

What do you think of using these as the Tube Statuses? I wanted to run them by you before I dive in on incorporating them into the ATN SC SIS. Let me know your thoughts.

 ** 

*Tube 9 Statuses:*
 * {+}Low Pressure{+}: Tube 9 air pressure (upper SAPT) is at or below 16.7 psia.
 * {+}Medium Pressure{+}: Tube 9 air pressure (upper SAPT) is above 16.7 psia +AND+ Tube 9 submerged pressure (lower SAPT) is at or below PC Intermediate target pressure.
 * {+}High Pressure{+}: Tube 9 submerged pressure (lower SAPT) is above PC Intermediate target pressure +AND+ is below the ordered depth sea pressure at the depth of the lower SAPT by at least 1.5 psi (exclusive).
 * {+}Full Pressure{+}: Tube 9 submerged pressure (lower SAPT) is below the ordered depth sea pressure at the depth of the lower SAPT by at most 1.5 psi (inclusive) +OR+ is above ordered depth sea pressure at the depth of the lower SAPT by at most 0.1 psi (inclusive).
 * {+}Above Sea Pressure{+}: Tube 9 submerged pressure (lower SAPT) is above the ordered depth sea pressure at the depth of the lower SAPT by at least 0.1 psi (exclusive).

A train of thoughts inspired by these TBRs:

 

Can anyone remind me of reasoning for why we don’t have a timeout interlock on ATN-2 and ATN-4 for WLC? Currently if you opened ATN-2 and tried to add air in WLC, but waterlevel didn’t drop because the top hatch is leaking air, you’d empty your whole air bank without receiving an alert that ABM isn’t working (until you got a low air bank alert at Ship Control).
 * We have interlocks to shut TD-803-(9) if an electrode is failing to be wetted or unwetted after 30 seconds, but we don’t have anything for if the waterlevel is outside the green band (and therefore WLC triggers action) but waterlevel is not at electrode level.
 * We should probably have an alert of some kind to let an operator know that WLC isn’t accomplishing any change in waterlevel in case that is an unexpected result (like in the case of top hatch leaking air).
 * We maybe don’t want an interlock to shut anything (because in a sinkout casualty, you might be failing to lower waterlevel but you’re at least slowing the rise of waterlevel, so the pressurization path should stay open) – but I guess that concern applies to our existing auto-shut timeout interlocks.
 * This kind of concern can be addressed in some cases (where the timeout interlock is on ATN-2 or ATN-4) by taking manual control of ATN-2 or ATN-4 at TCS. However, there are some timeout interlocks in Appendix A for TD-803-(9), and I can’t find anywhere in the SIS that mentions an option for manual control at TCS of TD-803-(9). Is this acceptable due to a hydraulic manual override to OPEN option for TD-803-(9)?

 

Thank you,

*Michael Kolakowski*

column1: TD - Investigate NTP Rollover Request with Originator & Our Network Engineer & Provide an Answer to D442
column37:
Cory, Zack and Jamie,

Could you please investigate whether your component uses NTP and whether it would be affected by 2036 issue?

 

Sincerely,

 

Yomen A Piscitelli



All,

Thank you for your responses on Y2038 problem, we appreciate your fast feedback! We would like to confirm whether or not your answers to Y2038 also accounted for NTP rollover in 2036. If not, please investigate that as well and get back to me with answers by 02/27/26 (Please don’t reply ALL).

A reminder on 2036: prior to the year 2038 problem, Network Time Protocol (NTP) will rollover in 2036. The subject issue is related to the handling of timestamps by some implementations of NTP.

 
 * NTP is a widely used protocol that enables synchronization of clocks between computer systems over a network. If your system does not use NTP, please reply that your system does not use NTP and ignore the rest of this email.
 * NTP protocol uses a 64-bit timestamp format, where the timestamp represents the number of seconds since 1/1/1900. The NTP epoch (starting point) is 1/1/1900 but there is another epoch 1/1/1970 (same as the Unix time epoch), which is more commonly used in modern computer systems. The difference in epochs leads to the NTP epoch being ahead of the Unix epoch.
 * The NTP 2036 rollover issue is concerned with the 32-bit version number field in NTP package. When this value rolls over to 0, it can potentially cause problems in NTP implementations.
 * The first rollover will occur on 2/7/2036, for which if NTP implementation is not accounted for correctly, it may result in incorrect or unpredictable behavior leading to time synchronization issues.
 * In order to mitigate the NTP rollover problem, system owners needs to ensure that their implementations are capable of handling 64-bit timestamps correctly and can handle rollover events smoothly (this can be done in a 32 bit environment, but it is not a native capability).

*+NOTES+*

In the interest of streamlining the review process examples of general comments identified below are not of consequence to the fidelity of a cable’s route.  Please refrain from these types of comments unless necessary.

 
 * Cable OD, weight/ft, and BR are automatically pulled from the cable information library. If there is a discrepancy between what we have on the cable info spreadsheet and HDBK-299, please comment with APPROVED OQE updating cable specs. (i.e. a letter updating hdbk-299)
 * Please do not comment on jack numbers or component DYPNs that are missing leading zeros. This is how excel automatically formats those numbers and the leading zeros are not of consequence when verifying that the correct components have been identified for a cable’s route
 * Please do not comment on ‘starting component’ vs ‘ending component.’ The decision to assign a component as ‘starting’ or ‘ending’ is done later by Ops and planning
 * Please do not comment on component name as long as the intent is met. (Cable DYPNs need to be correct and should be commented on with the exception of leading zeros)

 

Additionally, we’d like to create a greater emphasis on the end-to-end connectivity of a cable. (i.e. the whole route of the cable, not just it’s route through the subject disclosures). Moving forward, if your cables continue onto a disclosure that has a roadmap available for review by engineering, we encourage you to trace your cables through it and any other available roadmaps from component to component.

column305:
13/Apr/26 10:56 AM;zpryor;Per the TCS COD actuation times table, not only the times need to be updated but the explanation of the methodology of determining the component actuation times needs to be updated.
 # The table is based off max groom time meaning it includes the durations of all processes by which the component was groomed and excludes all processes that weren't involved in grooming.
 ## For example, the command timeout value includes TCS processing time if actuation during grooming was accomplished via the TCS. TCS processing time is excluded if the component was groomed by manually operating the control valve. The table does not include TCS processing times.
 # Per this statement, "In general, the command timeout fault timer starts when the component is no longer in the initial state as indicated by its sensors.     Start and stop triggers for the command timeout fault and grooming procedures are identical or to the greatest extent possible"
 ## The requirements need to be updated to include a condition of a change in state: The TCS shall detect a command timeout fault condition if the open state of the Tube 9 top hatch is not detected in less than or equal to 48 seconds of issuing an open command and the Tube 9 top hatch state changes from SHUT to IN TRANSITION."


 ## D413 concern is f the software lags and the actuator/mechanical components are working fine, how do you differentiate that the software caused the command timeout and not say something clogged?
 ### FHA deems a brief delay to be 2 seconds for software. There is not a clear way to differentiate between whether the software or the actual components caused the delay. However, in the TCS SSS additional time for TCS processing time/delay can be added should a brief delay cause an issue.

If during grooming or testing the TCS be used to determine the actuation time/groom time these numbers should be updated to include that;;;

column1: TD - GUI Strategy Action Meeting
column37:
For those not part of the GUI Strategy Meeting yesterday, we were assigned an action item to put together some slides in the next two weeks with a prototype of the bullets below. I would like to use this as a baseline to start our discussion. It includes initial concepts on addressing the asks. Please read through the below prior to the meeting.

{*}Action 1{*}: Camera Views to be dynamically allocated based on what they provide.

There are two approaches we should take for this.
 * Tube and Tray Control screens should be updated to contain an icon that when clicked would display live video feed of a subset of cameras. For example, clicking this icon near the Tube 10 bottom hatch will display the live video feed for relevant cameras.
 * We should put together Tube or Tray screen with a modified layout which by default displays live video feed. The exact view should be selectable by the operator.

 

{*}Action 2{*}: Concept behind better usage of the touch screens at the ROV workstations.

The touch screen should be used as a nominal operations touch screen. The touch screens should primarily contain controls. All needed statuses should be provided by the primary display in front of the operator. I would imagine the need to create modified UI Designs containing just the controls for Tube 10 Bottom hatch operations and Tray Auto Sub Mode operations.

 

{*}Action 3{*}: Moveable widgets, to give operators control over what their display would look like.

The intent behind this is clear. The operator would like some control over the layout of the screens in front of them. The best approach to present this concept would be for SW to put together a rough demonstration of this functionality to the operator.

 

{*}Action 4{*}: Situational Awareness Display
 * I believe Adam White has a concept and action to produce this. 

At the end of this meeting, we should be able to delegate out work towards creating the slides. 

{*}NOTE{*}: Everyone is not expected to stay for the full duration of the meeting. The end of the meeting will be reserved to allow Allen, Jacob, Zach, and I to collaborate on initial design work.

column1: TD - TCS Logic and Validity Initial Discussion w/ Software
column37:
Software and Test,

 

I sent a meeting out for 2/23 to discuss this topic of sensor validity and present some options, however we want to try to get some discussions started on this sooner than that. If we can get together this Monday that would be much appreciated.

 

From that invite:

“We need to sync to discuss the level of granularity that TCS SSS needs to write its requirements for sensor validity. This will cover statuses for redundant sensors and their associated logic, for example the Tube 9 upper and lower pressure statuses which are made up of tri-redundant SAPTS.

The Tube 9 upper and lower pressures are not only a calculated value, but that value is used for liquid level indication. If a sensor is faulted we want to allow the TCS to continue operations automatically by using sensor voting.

In this meeting Systems will present options of SAPT requirements and provide some background so that as a collective team (systems/software/test) we can decide at what level of granularity these requirements need to be written to get the correct implementation for the TCS. As well as where these requirements will need to live/the handoff between the SSS/SRS.”

 

Thanks,

Dylan LaMotte

 * Mechanical has kicked off a calc that will determine the value of hydro forces that Michael should use as new PE6 in the drafted calculation EC-413-2025-0037

column1: TD - SSN 812 Tube 10/VST and IBT CONOP during ROV loading Meeting Support
column37:
All,

 

Bringing up a topic that was discussed last year and had fallen to the bottom of my to do list. SSN 812 Tube 10/VST and IBT CONOP during ROV loading.

 

Background: Tube 10/VST and IBT will be flooded during the baseline plan to bottom load the ROV. With the ship in this condition, the freeboard will be low enough that all topside hatches will either need to be closed or have cofferdams installed. This is a considerable burden on the facility where the ROV loading operation will occur that we would like to avoid. The desired outcome is to develop a CONOP that would enable enough of the IBT to be filled with air during an ROV bottom load that the ship sits high enough in the water for topside hatches to be open.

 

The high level CONOP that was previously discussed: Start with tube 10/VST and IBT dry, keep vent path shut, align flood/drain pump, flood tube 10, open equalize path, open bottom hatch

 

D413 (Hesser) suggested detailed CONOP:
 # Override position of TD-803-(10) to OPEN, but leave valve SHUT
 # Align all remaining TCS controlled SSW FD valves as necessary to meet FLOOD READY permissive prereqs
 # Send FLOOD READY permissive to SCS
 # SCS verify that all potential vent paths on IBT are isolated, and hawsepipe seals are released
 # SCS align remaining valves for flooding and flood tube to height of 23 – 28 ft ABL. Tube and IBT pressurize to a few psig.
 # Secure flooding.
 # TCS send E/D permissive to SCS
 # SCS align valves for equalizing, tube/IBT pressure drops a bit, water level falls a bit, tube is equalized
 # TCS override position of TD-809 and TD-835 to OPEN to meet Align to Sea criteria, but SCS leave valves SHUT
 # TCS open bottom hatch

 

D440 (Sevigny) response/concern:

As far as the CONOPS, the first step is the only one that gives me pause. We only use overrides to enforce the true state of a system at sea. This would be using the system in a way it wasn’t designed or intended for. Not saying we can’t as you could literally just do it, nothing stops you, but this is not how overrides are intended to be used. I would want safety to buy off on this as well. Once you start telling the system that things are in positions or conditions they aren’t, it’s possible to get unintended consequences, satisfying or enabling functionality based on the override. There could be other ways to do this like interlock suppression or a maintenance mode. However the juice might not be worth the squeeze depending on the frequency of the evolution.

23/Feb/26 8:51 AM;zpryor;Hello James and Dylan,

 

I suspect Ship Control is going to need the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism ENGAGED signal in addition to the LOCKED signal we already have for our hull openings indications. Concur, SCS will use the interlock ENGAGED status for hull closure (1TR) instead of locking ring status.

 

Looking at the TCS SSS (TCS-2378), in seems like the following is needed to know the Tube 9 bottom hatch is closed:
 * bottom hatch is SHUT (Ship control assumes shut based on Locked signal)
 * hatch locking ring is LOCKED (Ship Control receives this signal)
 * interlock mechanism is ENGAGED  (may be needed by Ship Control)

 

To aid my understanding, could you please provide answers to the following questions?:
 # Our previous assumption was that the bottom hatch can't be OPEN (hatch position) while the locking ring is LOCKED due to mechanical interlocks. Is this still true? Yes.
 # Can we have a situation where the interlock mechanism solenoid is ENGAGED and the locking mechanism is not LOCKED? For example, software failure or failure to follow manual control procedures. No. The interlock mechanism can only ENAGAGE when the locking ring is LOCKED.
 # What would happen if the ship submerges with the interlock mechanism solenoid DISENGAGED? Flood risk? Technically as long as the hatch is shut were not going to flood. However Interlock ENGAGED is the new hull closure signal, as this is the normal state while submerged.

 

Let me know if you agree or I am misunderstanding anything.

 

For reference here is TCS-2378:

 

The Tube 9 bottom hatch shut sequence shall follow the order of operations below.

 
 # Command the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring to the UNLOCKED position to ensure the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring is unlocked prior to shutting the hatch.

 
 # Energize the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism DISENGAGE solenoid to ensure the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism is disengaged prior to shutting the hatch.

 
 # After the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring is UNLOCKED and the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism is DISENGAGED, de-energize the Tube 9 bottom hatch OPEN solenoid and energize the Tube 9 bottom hatch SHUT solenoid.

 
 # Once the Tube 9 bottom hatch is SHUT, then after a 3 second delay command the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring to the LOCKED position.

 
 # After the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring is LOCKED, de-energize the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism DISENGAGE solenoid and energize the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism ENGAGE solenoid.

 
 # After the Tube 9 bottom hatch interlock mechanism is ENGAGED, command the Tube 9 bottom hatch locking ring EMAs to FULLY DEPOWER. 

 

 

Regards,

 

*Ruri Galvan*;;;

 * Invoking elements defined in the style guide within GUI Spec requirements, style guide consumes HMI Spec directly

Style requirements are those that have to do with the static appearance of the objects such as colors, shape, font, sizes, contrast. 

These will be displayed and known in the style guide, but there may not be requirements for the items.

Posted on: Wed Dec 10 12:39:40 EST 2025
All of the time tracked to this item not just is for the time spent to provide a response but also includes time needed to review what a Kalman filter is that the NAVSEA representative suggested the TCS could utilize to calculated average liquid level in Tube 9 and review the current process by which the TCS plans to calculated liquid level in Tube 9 which involves a low pass filter.

The TCS plans to calculate liquid level by correcting the SAPT measurements by translating to the center of the tube to negate water slosh from pitch and roll, taking the average or median of the upper and lower sensor values, filtering out the noise through a low pass filter, and then through a differential pressure calculation between the filtered upper and lower pressures calculate an accurate liquid level through a hydrostatic pressure equation based on the static water head indicated by the differential pressure value. That instantaneous liquid level can then be averaged over a specified time interval to sufficiently track the change in Tube 9 liquid level the TCS needs to react.

column37:
Originally the electrodes we were using before becoming obsolete used an FSS-2 cable which lead to a special case EMI classification for the R6-1 signal coming from them. However, since we are procuring new electrodes that has brought the opportunity to change the cable type to a non-special case EMI cable (TSS-3).

After talking with the vendor and Allen Ly's investigation it appears the vendor can create the electrodes with the TSS-3 cable and overmold the connector side as well.

As for procurement specifications, it looks like we might be able to avoid one. If we point to the relevant specifications for each part of the set up (point to Electrode Spec., point to 24231/X spec for connector, point to 915/X spec for cable), we can just make note of that in the PO. 

However, there is one thing that should be noted, since I think it may mean we have to either change cable type, or modify the drawing/specification for the electrode. Jesse pointed out to make sure the 16AWG wires would fit inside the terminal piece. In short, I don’t think it fits, because 2 leads need to be soldered into the terminal based on the diagram. 2 leads stacked together would be roughly 0.115”, but the terminal opening is roughly 0.11”, so I don’t think it’ll fit. We can either choose a different cable type, OR make a modification to the original drawing/specification of the electrode to make a bigger drill hole for the terminal, which might be a big enough change to warrant a specification.
